Easily the most bipolar physics/collision I've ever seen. Pulling teammates requires you to hover over them and press the 'E' key, and with 3 people you often end up at angles where you can only select the person standing safe next to you. Even worse, hitboxes often push you off at the smallest touch, forcing you away and your team with you. One of us was having PC problems, so the slightest bit of lag - while otherwise still allowing a window to react - would mean the briefest hiccup of his character's momentum turned him into a tungsten anvil, and thereby us with him straight down.
These 3 factors, coupled with the umbrella lack of fine tuning that comes with most asset flips by nature, makes the game effectively impossible.

Rage games, at their best, shift the onus to you through an error YOU made - however troll-y the situation might be - and it ultimately falls to your skill to react and/or adapt to find a way forward; it operates with a consistent set of rules at its bottom line.
Here, you're constantly fighting the engine itself as it kicks you in the balls and then again while you're down. There is no sense of "I could have done that better," it's "when will it let me do this."
[i]Elden Ring[/i], for example, is a point of contention for a lot of players as to where it falls between the two, but it also doesn't require the precision of a parkour platformer. A game like [i]Getting Over It[/i] or [i]Only Up[/i] adheres enough to those other principles for it to be fun - each allowing your precision to build off of the game's - and wanting to beat yourself up more than you it.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the game lacks random matchmaking and requires players to already have a group to play together.

citations.review_text:
I bought this thinking there would be random matchmaking.

There is not.

That single realization basically destroyed the entire purchase for me because the whole appeal was imagined chaos with strangers. Without that, the experience becomes heavily dependent on already having a group willing to engage in coordinated suffering.

And if you don’t?

You mostly just stare at the install icon wondering why you bought it.

Not recommended.

The game looks really great, and I bought it when it came on sale (even though it costs about the same as two meals in my country), but unfortunately I couldn't play the game with my friends. Every time we entered together and progressed a little, the game would kick us out or kick one of us . We tried for half an hour of playing and couldn't, so I got a refund.

An extremely fun, though equally janky, friendslop experience. The gameplay is simple enough; it's a platformer, where you're (as the name says) chained together with your fellow player. This requires extreme communication, precision, and timing, and it's quite enjoyable, even if it's laugh inducingly 'frustrating' haha.

Playing this game with a friend on call is basically essential. Communication is key, and the game even aids the player in this with the inclusion of a countdown button to really nail precise timing. 

However, the game can be fairly janky with occasional hitbox detection hiccups, connection issues even with good internet, and the odd graphical bug here and there. Still, it's not enough to ruin the game.

Graphically and sound wise, everything but the silly and cheesy voice acting for god and the devil, are all clearly stock assets. Basically everything you see in game is what I am guessing a purchased and reused game asset from some online graphical asset store. Though I will say, even with that being the case, all the different environments are fun to look at and jump around.

Overall, I do recommend the game if you want a fun, short enough friendslop experience. Just don't go in expecting much replay value or the game to be a masterpiece of multiplayer or anything. It's a cheap bit of enjoyment, silliness, and playful """frustration""" (see; absolutely hilarious failures that'll ensue) to play with someone you care about!
Game needs serious optimizations but other than that, its fun.

As someone who's played a lot of platformers, I went into this feeling overconfident. I've beaten Alt+F4 from start to finish and spent way too many hours on old-school Roblox obby games, so I thought this would be a breeze... or so I thought.

Then my girlfriend joined in. It wouldn't really be Chained Together if I played it alone, right?

That's when the real challenge began. Parts that would've been easy solo suddenly became frustrating because all it takes is one mistimed jump from either of you, and you're both paying the price. There were definitely moments where I was losing my mind.

We weren't brave enough to try Normal mode since it has no checkpoints, so we stuck with Beginner. Even then, the amount of backtracking after every fall could get pretty brutal. The checkpoints helped, but they didn't stop the frustration of repeating sections over and over.

It took us around 6 hours to finish, and despite all the suffering, I genuinely had a great time. It's chaotic, hilarious, and incredibly satisfying when you finally make it past a section you've been stuck on.

As for my girlfriend... I'm not entirely sure she'd recommend it. I think some of those levels took years off her life.
